questions.q: What are the two directions of growth a vector database in production actually has to scale for?
options: More data (vectors stored) and more throughput (queries per second / concurrent users)
More programming languages and more file formats
More embedding models and more distance metrics
More chapters in the documentation and more tutorials
questions.explain: A RAG pipeline that works in a demo can hit two separate walls in production: the collection growing far larger, and far more queries arriving at once — scaling has to address both.

questions.q: According to the real formula shown in this lesson (memory_size = vectors * dims * 4 bytes * 1.5), roughly how much RAM does 1,000,000 vectors at 1,536 dimensions need?
options: About 900 MB
About 92 GB
About 1.5 TB
About 9.2 GB
questions.explain: 1,000,000 x 1,536 x 4 x 1.5 = 9,216,000,000 bytes, or roughly 9.2 GB — this is Qdrant's own published estimate formula for a collection's memory footprint.

questions.q: What is vertical scaling, as shown on the real Qdrant Cloud "Scale your cluster" screen in this lesson?
options: Adding more nodes and sharding the collection across them
Giving each existing node more RAM, CPU, or disk — simple, but with a ceiling and usually a rolling restart
Deleting old vectors to free up space
Switching from HNSW to IVF indexing
questions.explain: Vertical scaling increases the resources on the nodes you already have, which is simple but bounded by a single machine's maximum size.

questions.q: What does horizontal scaling add, that vertical scaling doesn't provide?
options: A higher distance-metric accuracy
A smaller embedding dimensionality
More nodes with the collection sharded across them, plus replication, and no hard capacity ceiling
Automatic translation of stored documents
questions.explain: Horizontal scaling adds nodes and splits (shards) the collection across them, with replicated copies for availability — removing the single-machine ceiling that vertical scaling runs into.

questions.q: Why does the lesson emphasize monitoring (the real Metrics screen shown) rather than guessing when to scale?
options: Real-time RAM, CPU, and disk metrics show resource pressure building before it turns into an outage
Because monitoring is legally required by every cloud provider
Because metrics automatically fix performance problems without any action needed
Because the index rebuilds itself whenever metrics are viewed
questions.explain: A managed console's Metrics tab gives visibility into resource usage trends over a chosen time window, which is what tells you a cluster needs to scale before it actually runs out of headroom.
